sources.citation: Fergus I.M. Craik, Robert S. Lockhart (1972). Levels of processing: A framework for memory research. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior.
sources.notes: Foundational primary study (1972) in Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior establishing the core experimental paradigm and quantitative parameters.

sources.citation: Fergus I.M. Craik, Michael J. Watkins (1973). The role of rehearsal in short-term memory. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior.
sources.notes: Craik & Watkins's 1973 demonstration that prolonged Type-I maintenance rehearsal alone fails to boost long-term free recall.

sources.citation: Michael W. Eysenck (1978). Levels of processing: A reply to Lockhart and Craik. British Journal of Psychology.
sources.notes: Subsequent empirical and theoretical investigation (1978) in British Journal of Psychology extending the foundational findings.

sources.citation: Fergus I. M. Craik, Endel Tulving (1975). Depth of processing and the retention of words in episodic memory. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General.
sources.notes: Craik & Tulving's 1975 ten-experiment empirical test showing incidental recall climbs from ~17% (case) to ~48% (rhyme) to >80% (sentence meaning).

sources.citation: C. Donald Morris, John D. Bransford, Jeffery J. Franks (1977). Levels of processing versus transfer appropriate processing. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior.
sources.notes: Morris, Bransford & Franks (1977 JVLVB) Transfer-Appropriate Processing experiments demonstrating rhyme encoding outperforms semantic encoding on rhyme-cued tests.

sources.citation: Anthony D. Wagner, Daniel L. Schacter, Michael Rotte, Wilma Koutstaal, Anat Maril, Anders M. Dale, Bruce R. Rosen, Randy L. Buckner (1998). Building Memories: Remembering and Forgetting of Verbal Experiences as Predicted by Brain Activity. Science.
sources.notes: Event-related fMRI subsequent-memory study showing that trial-by-trial left inferior prefrontal and parahippocampal activation during semantic encoding predicts later recall.
